name: Freya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We grow leeks, carrots and broccoli on about two hundred hectares, nearly all of it for two big supermarket chains. My partner Jonas's family has farmed it for three generations, and I joined two years ago. Right now it's leek season, so I'm in the field by six with the harvest crew, then in the packhouse checking that every box meets the supermarket's spec sheet, which is their rulebook for size, colour and even how much mud is allowed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before you joined?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I taught nine-year-olds for fifteen years at the primary school on Station Road. When Jonas's dad had his heart scare, we decided I'd come in and run the people side, the crew and the paperwork. I'm good with people and a total beginner with crops; last spring I signed off a whole trailer of broccoli that was too loose in the head and the buyer sent it back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the crew, honestly. Most of them come from abroad for the season, and we've got Andrei and his wife who've been coming for nine years and send our kids birthday cards. What wears me out is the buyer calling at four in the afternoon to cut tomorrow's order by a third, after we've already pulled it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, and I already use it a bit. I put messages for the crew into a translation tool so the Romanian and Nepali lads get the shift times right. So, a better search engine, sure, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes almost nothing for me. The supermarket will keep squeezing us like it always has. AI doesn't change who holds the pen on the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my tractor driving certificate, which I've been putting off since summer. And I'd get the second packhouse fridge fixed before Christmas, it's about four thousand. Probably use the AI thing to help write the audit notes, because those take me a whole Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing on this card keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the buyer cutting orders. What happens to the leeks you've already pulled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some go to a wholesaler at half the price and some go to the food bank in town. The rest go back on the field as compost. Jonas just goes quiet and walks off to the workshop, and I've learned not to follow him for an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings, your pension. Do they change how you see any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They do. I've got my teacher's pension building up, and we've got over a year of money put by, plus the land. I know a lot of the crew send every penny home, so I try not to sound smug about being calm.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and I already use it a little, translating shift messages for the crew. A better search engine is fine by me.
S0.think: Honestly I think it changes almost nothing for us. The supermarket will keep squeezing like it always has, and AI doesn't change who holds the pen on the contract.
S0.do: Finishes her tractor driving certificate and gets the second packhouse fridge repaired before Christmas for about four thousand. Tries an AI tool to help write the supermarket audit notes that eat her Sundays.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing on the card that would keep her awake.
S0.quote: AI doesn't change who holds the pen on the contract.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is aware of her own comfort and checks herself against the crew who send their wages home. Her real opponent in every answer is the supermarket buyer. She already uses AI in small, practical ways and doesn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need proper apprenticeships, paid for by the state, not left to whichever company feels generous. I'd probably share some article about it online and get into an argument with my cousin. Same as I did when they closed the teacher training course at the local college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the supermarkets will use it first, on their side. Better forecasts, tighter orders, and every mistake pushed back down onto us. I'm a slow learner on the farm side, so a buyer with a clever computer worries me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the other growers in the co-op do, then try the same software. Jonas's friend Karl already uses one to plan which field gets cut which day. I'd give it a season before I trusted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a slow leak rather than a burst pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'every mistake pushed back down onto us'. Give me an example.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last July the buyer's system said hot weather meant salads, not broccoli, so they cut us by forty percent on a Tuesday. We had it cut and cooled already. In this picture, I imagine that happening every week, but faster and more polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would hiring fewer beginners touch the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the packhouse, where the young local kids start on the grading line. Our neighbour's daughter Maja did a summer there and now she's doing agricultural science. If that first rung goes, we lose the Majas.

S1.say: I'd say this is when we need proper apprenticeships paid for by the state, not left to whichever company feels generous. I'd share articles online and argue with my cousin about it.
S1.think: Privately I think the supermarkets will use it first, on their side, with tighter orders and every mistake pushed down onto us. A buyer with a clever computer worries me more than any robot.
S1.do: Waits to see what other co-op growers adopt, then trials the same field-planning software that Karl uses. Gives it a full season before relying on it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a slow leak rather than a burst pipe.
S1.quote: In this picture, I imagine that happening every week, but faster and more polite.
S1.fieldNote: She sees AI mainly as a tool for the powerful side of the contract, and the July broccoli story makes that concrete. Her steady streak shows clearly: she follows the co-op and gives it a season. She thinks about the bottom rung of the ladder like a teacher would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in for the office workers, with retraining that's real and not a website. And I'd say it at the school gate, because half the parents there work in offices in town. I'd join the union petition if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my old colleagues worry me more than I worry for myself. Schools have lots of admin staff, and the woman in our office, Pam, has been there twenty years. On the farm, I think we just carry on, and maybe the supermarket's paperwork gets more annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Pam with a reference or whatever she needs, honestly that's the first thing. On the farm I'd hold off on the new packing line until the dust settles, that's sixty thousand we don't need to spend this year. And I'd start using the AI tool more for the audits, because if the buyer's side is all machines, I want mine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty. I left the office world just before it caught fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want your own AI if the buyer has theirs. Isn't that what you were worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, it is. I don't love it, but I'm not going to bring a pencil to that fight. I'd use it the way I use a calculator, not the way Jonas uses the radio, which is all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ella is fourteen and wants to be a lawyer, so I'd tell her to keep her options wide. Rasmus is ten and only cares if the tractor is still there. I'd tell him yes, the tractor's still there.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in with real retraining for office workers, not just a website. I'd say it at the school gate and sign any union petition going.
S2.think: Privately my old colleagues worry me more than I worry for myself, people like Pam in the school office. On the farm I think we carry on, with more annoying paperwork from the supermarket.
S2.do: Helps her former colleague Pam with a reference first. Delays the sixty-thousand packing line until things settle and starts using AI more for audits to match the buyer's side.
S2.feel: Uneasy and a little guilty, as though she left office life just before it caught fire.
S2.quote: I don't love it, but I'm not going to bring a pencil to that fight.
S2.fieldNote: When I pointed out the contradiction about using AI against AI, she laughed and owned it. Her instincts are public and collective, yet her own moves are careful and practical. Her daughter's legal ambitions gave the first sign of worry about her own family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the gains should go to everyone, through taxes on the AI companies and the people whose shares are booming. Free school meals, better care, a fair wage for the people who grow the food. I'd go to a march, which I haven't done since I was twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about Ella. She wants to be a lawyer and this card says lawyers lose their jobs. And our land would be worth a fortune on paper, which feels like winning a prize for something we didn't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Ella and look at courses that still need people in the room, like nursing or teaching or agricultural science, without scaring her. I'd talk to Jonas about whether we take on more land from neighbours who sell up. And I'd stop the extra mortgage payments for a year and keep the cash, because a political crisis means anything can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly about Ella. And angry in a tired way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If town people are losing jobs, what happens to your sales?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still eat leeks, but they'd buy the cheapest ones. The supermarket would push its own cheap line harder and squeeze our price again. I think we'd be fine but thinner, like the end of a long winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the crew? Would they still come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there's a crisis in their own countries, more might come, not fewer. Andrei told me once his nephew is an accountant in Bucharest. In this picture, his nephew might be in my leek field next September.

S3.say: I'd say loudly that the gains should go to everyone, through taxes on AI companies and on the people whose shares are booming. I'd march for it, which I haven't done since I was twenty.
S3.think: Privately I think about my daughter Ella, who wants to be a lawyer when this card says lawyers lose their jobs. And our land being worth a fortune on paper feels like a prize for something we didn't do.
S3.do: Talks with Ella about hands-on careers like nursing, teaching or agricultural science, gently. Pauses extra mortgage payments for a year to hold cash, and discusses buying land from neighbours who sell.
S3.feel: Anxious, mostly for her daughter, and angry in a tired way.
S3.quote: In this picture, his nephew might be in my leek field next September.
S3.fieldNote: The worry shifts from the farm to her daughter's future, and that's where the emotion is. She is uncomfortable gaining from rising land values and says so plainly. The detail about Andrei's accountant nephew shows she thinks about the crew as people with families, not as labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in the fields must come with rules: a share of the savings to the workers, and training paid for by whoever buys the machines. I'd write to the growers' association. I'd also say, slightly less politely, that the supermarkets will take the savings and give us nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one where my job goes. I'm the crew supervisor, and if a machine pulls leeks there's no crew to supervise. Jonas would still have the farm, but I'd be the one who's no use, because I can't fix machines and I'm still learning to drive the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for Karl or another co-op grower to try a picking robot first, I'm not betting the farm on a prototype. Meanwhile I'd do a course in machine maintenance at the college in town, about two evenings a week. And I'd talk to Andrei honestly about next season, because he deserves to plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, which surprised me when I said it. I feel like I'd just found my place and now it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Andrei?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, if the machines come, we'll need people to run them and fix them, and I'd rather it was you than a stranger. I'd mean it, but I don't know if Jonas could afford to pay him all year round. Honestly, I'd probably cry, and he'd make a joke to stop me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which costs would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids' holiday to the coast, about three thousand, and the new car we've been talking about. Not the crew's wages while they're still here. And not Ella's tutoring, whatever happens.

S4.say: I'd say robots in the fields must come with rules: a share of the savings for workers and training paid for by whoever buys the machines. I'd also say the supermarkets will take the savings and give us nothing.
S4.think: Privately this is the one where my job goes, because if a machine pulls leeks there's no crew to supervise. Jonas would still have the farm, but I'd be the one who's no use.
S4.do: Waits for a co-op grower to trial picking robots first, then signs up for two evenings a week of machine maintenance at the college. Talks honestly with Andrei about next season and cuts the three-thousand family holiday before any crew wages.
S4.feel: Frightened, which surprised her, as if she had just found her place and now it's going.
S4.quote: I feel like I'd just found my place and now it's going.
S4.fieldNote: Robots are what turn her worry from other people to herself, and her voice changed when she said it. She still waits for others to go first, but her own plan is to retrain into the machines. Loyalty to Andrei and the crew is real and costly for her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, definitely, because that's the one where I'm the person who isn't needed. What would help is training that's free and in the evenings, near home, and some rule that the supermarkets can't take every penny the machines save. And proper support for the crew, wherever they come from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the food itself. Nobody asks who decides what a leek is worth, and it's three people in an office two hundred kilometres away. If AI is going to be anywhere, it'll be in that office first, and nobody in my field will get a vote.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who decides what a leek is worth, and it's three people in an office two hundred kilometres away.
portrait: Freya Olsen is a former primary school teacher who joined her partner's family vegetable farm two years ago to run the harvest crew and the supermarket paperwork. She's warm, quick to laugh at her own contradictions, and sees the supermarket buyer, not AI, as the real power over her life. Through the office scenarios she worries for former colleagues and her daughter's career more than herself. In the robot picture she sees her own supervisor role disappear and plans, carefully and after others go first, to retrain in machine maintenance while standing by her long-time crew.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because a machine that harvests leeks leaves no crew for her to supervise.
whatWouldHelp: Free evening training close to home, rules stopping supermarkets from taking all the savings robots bring, and proper support for the crew.
